deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous prose passage in German, in the style of lecture or school notes on Greek history. It continues from folio 96, which covers the restoration of Athens under Thrasybulus and Spartan hegemony, and runs into folio 98 (Coronea, Cnidus, the Peace of Antalcidas).

Content of folio 97, in order:
1. Sparta, answering the appeal of the Ionian Greek cities, declares war on Persia.
2. The Spartans invade Asia Minor under Thimbron; the margin gives the year 399.
3. The next year Dercyllidas succeeds him. He exploits the quarrels between the Persian satraps, brings Tissaphernes to a separate peace, and attacks Pharnabazus alone. The scribe corrected 'Fer-' to 'Phar-nabatz'.
4. In 396 Agesilaus, the Spartan king and 'one of the greatest generals', takes over. In spring 396 he crosses to Asia, plans to overthrow the Persian throne, and makes his headquarters at Ephesus. He forms a cavalry, raids Phrygia, and comes to know Persian conditions (probably 'Persiens Schwäche').
5. In 395 he pushes into the interior of Asia Minor; the satraps try to win him over by negotiation.
6. In 394 a 7-year war against Sparta begins (the Corinthian War). The Spartans send Lysander to Boeotia, where he falls at Haliartus.

There are no formulas, computations, figures or numerical work beyond historical dates. The hand and subject matter suggest a student's or auditor's notes bound into the bundle, not Gauss's own mathematical work. Nothing can be reconstructed mathematically.
errors: Historical, not mathematical: the Corinthian War is usually dated from 395 BC, not 394 BC.
Historical, not mathematical: Lysander fell at Haliartus in 395 BC, so placing it after a war beginning in 394 is slightly out of order.
Historical, not mathematical: 'a 7-year war' is consistent with 394-387 but conventionally the war runs 395-387 (8 years).
deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical prose about Spartan-Persian conflict (399-394 BC) in a lecture-notes style, with no mathematical content. It is very likely not even Gauss's own composition.
transcription_corrections: Line 12: 'zu schmeißen[?]' — the reading 'schmeißen' fits the letter forms. It follows 'den persischen Thron über den Haufen', so the sense is 'to overthrow'.

Line 15: 'lernte[?] persische Gebiete[?] kennen' — the image more plausibly reads 'lernte Persiens Schwäche kennen' (the first word begins with a Kurrent P and ends in -ens). This also matches the historical narrative.
Line 10: 'glänzende' is clearly written with an umlaut-type mark over the a (rendered 'glänzende'); the reading is confirmed.
Line 5: a comma or caret insertion follows 'benutzte'; 'er' is inserted above the line before 'zum Separatfrieden'. The transcription handles this correctly.
Line 6: 'Fer-' is struck through with 'Phar' written above, giving 'Pharnabatz' (Pharnabazus). The transcription is correct.
